498.title: The divine messengers
498.hook: Yama asks: didn't you see the baby, the old, the sick, the dead?
498.howItsDone: Buddhists often reflect on aging, sickness and death as everyday reminders to practice, and the four sights of the young Siddhartha are retold at festivals and in temple murals across Buddhist countries.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bala, the fool's three pains, and your line, the turtle and the yoke.

A smoke alarm chirps. Low battery. You think: I'll deal with it later. It chirps again a week later, and again a week after that. Every chirp is a message, and none of them shouts. The hundred and thirtieth discourse imagines a person after death, brought before Yama, the king of the dead in Indian tradition. Yama doesn't open with a list of crimes. He asks questions. Good man, didn't you see the first messenger of the gods when it appeared among people? And the person says: no, sir, I didn't.
screen: `A SMOKE ALARM CHIRPS.` → `BEFORE KING YAMA.` → `DIDN'T YOU SEE THE MESSENGER?`

segments.voice: Then Yama explains. Didn't you ever see a tiny baby, lying helpless in its own mess? And didn't it occur to you: I too was born; let me do good while I can? The second messenger: an old person, eighty, ninety, a hundred, bent like a roof beam, leaning on a stick, trembling. The third: someone sick, in pain, lifted and laid down by others. The fourth: someone caught for a crime and punished. The fifth: a dead body, a day or two or three gone. Each time Yama asks the same thing: didn't it occur to you that you are subject to this too? Then the line at the center. This harm wasn't done by your mother or father, your brother or sister, your friends, your relatives, or the gods. You did it, and you will feel its fruit. It's stern. But listen to who these messengers are. Not angels with trumpets. A baby. A grandparent. A patient. A body. They appear among ordinary people every day. Many Buddhists hear an echo of the four sights that, in the traditional life story, moved young Siddhartha to leave the palace: an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering monk. And the discourse ends with a surprise: Yama himself wishes he could be born human, hear a Buddha teach, and understand. Even the judge of the dead wants the chance the living have.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you saw recently, an infant in a stroller, an older neighbor on the stairs, a friend who's ill, and let them be a messenger, not of fear, but of a plain fact: I'm a body too, and this time is limited. 499.title: One fine night
499.hook: don't chase the past, don't pin hopes on the future; see what is here, today
499.carry: see it clearly, right where it is
499.howItsDone: The bhaddekaratta verse is chanted in some Theravada monasteries, and meditation teachers in several traditions use it to teach dwelling in the present moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: devaduta, the messengers of the gods: a baby, an elder, someone sick, someone punished, a body. Your line: the messengers came.

Ten minutes in old photos pulls the mood one way. Ten minutes planning next year pulls it another. In both, the room you're sitting in has gone missing. The hundred and thirty-first discourse is short, and at its heart is a verse of just a few lines. The Buddha recites it at Jeta's Grove near Savatthi, then explains it. And it won't stay in one discourse: the next three come back to it.
screen: `TEN MINUTES IN OLD PHOTOS.` → `TEN MINUTES IN NEXT YEAR.` → `A SHORT VERSE, EXPLAINED.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Don't chase after the past. Don't build your hopes on the future. The past is already left behind; the future hasn't come. Whatever is present, see it clearly, right where it is, steady and unshaken. Do today what needs doing, with energy. Who knows, death may come tomorrow, and there's no bargaining with death and his great army. Whoever lives this way, keen, day and night, the peaceful sage calls one who has had a bhaddekaratta. Bhadda means good or auspicious. Eka means one. Ratta is the hard part: it's usually read as night, but translators don't agree on the whole, so you'll find one fine night, a single excellent night, or an auspicious day. The shape of the teaching is clear, though. The Buddha explains how people chase the past: I had such a body, such feelings, such thoughts, and they find delight there. How they build hopes on the future: I'll have such a body, such feelings. And how, in the present, they take body or feeling or mind as a self, and get pulled along. The one who doesn't is the one having that fine night. Not a night of special visions. A night, or a day, lived where it actually is. After yesterday's messengers, this is the answer: not fear, but full attention to the only day there is.

segments.voice: Sit a while, and each time the mind slides into a memory, say softly: past; each time it jumps to a plan: future. Then come back to what's actually here: this breath, this sound, this weight. You don't have to hate the past or the future; you're just choosing, for now, the room you're in.

500.title: The verse explained
500.hook: Ananda, Mahakaccana and Lomasakangiya each explain the same verse
500.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics memorize and chant short verses and study the commentaries that explain them; the bhaddekaratta verse is among those chanted in some communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhaddekaratta, one fine night, a short verse about living where you are. Your line: see it clearly, right where it is.
screen: `SEE IT CLEARLY, RIGHT WHERE IT IS.`

segments.voice: Five hundred days. A line heard on day ten can come back differently on day four hundred. Same words, new weight. The next three discourses take yesterday's verse and pass it through four monks. One teaches it from memory. Two first hear of it from a deity, and don't know it. And one explains it when the Buddha leaves it unexplained. It's almost a study in how a teaching travels.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED DAYS.` → `SAME WORDS, NEW WEIGHT.` → `ONE VERSE, FOUR MONKS.`

segments.voice: In the hundred and thirty-second discourse, Ananda teaches the verse and its explanation to the monks in the assembly hall. The Buddha later asks who taught it, and confirms Ananda got it right. Ananda had heard it and kept it. In the hundred and thirty-third, a monk named Samiddhi goes to bathe at some hot springs near Rajagaha. A deity appears at night and asks: do you know the bhaddekaratta verse? No. Learn it, says the deity. So Samiddhi asks the Buddha, who recites only the verse and goes inside. The monks are left with a short poem and no explanation. They go to Mahakaccana, known for unpacking the Buddha's brief sayings. He explains it through the senses: you chase the past when your mind is bound by desire to what the eye once saw, thinking, such was my eye, such were the sights. You build on the future when you set your heart on what the eye will see. The Buddha hears this and says: if you'd asked me, I'd have explained it the same way. In the hundred and thirty-fourth, a monk named Lomasakangiya is asked about the verse by a deity named Candana. He doesn't know it. But Candana does, and recites it, saying the Buddha once taught it to the gods. So Lomasakangiya walks all the way to Savatthi to hear it properly. Three discourses, three ways of meeting the same few lines, and one line they all carry: do today what needs doing, with energy. In Pali, ajja eva kiccam atappam: today itself, the ardent effort.

501.title: Why lives differ
501.hook: why some are short-lived, some sickly, some wise: deeds
501.howItsDone: The same words, owner and heir of one's deeds, close the five recollections of AN 5.57, which Theravada monastics and lay people recite as a daily reflection; teachers also caution against using kamma to blame people for illness or poverty.

segments.voice: Yesterday: atappa, ardent effort, the line Ananda, Mahakaccana and Lomasakangiya all carried. Your line: today, the effort.

Two kids are born in the same hospital on the same night. One grows up healthy and comfortable; the other struggles with illness and money for years. Why? A young brahmin named Subha, Todeyya's son, put that question to the Buddha. You met Subha a few weeks ago, asking about the way to Brahma. Here, in the hundred and thirty-fifth discourse, he lays out seven pairs. Why are some short-lived and some long-lived? Sickly and healthy? Plain and beautiful? Powerless and influential? Poor and rich? Low-born and high-born? Foolish and wise?
screen: `SAME HOSPITAL, SAME NIGHT.` → `SUBHA, TODEYYA'S SON.` → `SEVEN PAIRS OF LIVES.`

segments.voice: The Buddha first answers in one dense line, paraphrased here: beings are owners of their deeds, heirs of their deeds. They're born of their deeds, bound to their deeds, and have their deeds as their refuge. It's deeds, kamma, that sort beings into lower and higher. Subha says: I don't understand that in brief. Please explain. So the Buddha goes pair by pair, as the text frames it, across lives. One who kills and is cruel tends toward a short life; one who refrains, a long one. One who harms others with fist or stick, toward sickness; one who doesn't, health. Quick anger, toward a plain appearance; patience, beauty. Envy, toward little influence. Not giving, toward poverty. Arrogance, refusing to honor those worthy of honor, toward low birth. And not asking the wise what's good and what's harmful, toward foolishness. That last one is worth a second look: wisdom, here, grows from asking questions, which is exactly what Subha is doing. The tradition reads this as how actions tend to ripen, not a ledger for judging anyone. Nothing in the discourse invites anyone to look at a sick neighbor and call them guilty, and tomorrow's discourse warns against simple readings. But the teaching has a hopeful edge. If beings are heirs of their deeds, then what anyone does now is the inheritance they're writing. Subha, at the end, goes for refuge. The question he asked about other lives turned into a question about his own.
screen: `OWNERS AND HEIRS OF DEEDS` · `PAIR BY PAIR, ACROSS LIVES` · `WISDOM GROWS FROM ASKING` · `NOT A LEDGER FOR JUDGING` · then, large: `HEIRS OF OUR DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing you did a while ago, a kindness, a sharp word, a promise kept or broken, and trace what grew from it: a friendship that's easier, a silence that's still there. Don't judge yourself; just see the line from deed to fruit. Then rest with the breath, and notice that this sitting is a deed too.
Kammadayada. Heir of one's deeds: the Buddha's answer to Subha, that beings are owners and heirs of their deeds, and deeds shape how lives unfold. Today's word.
Your line: heirs of our deeds. It's a line for looking at your own life, never for judging someone else's. Until tomorrow.

502.title: More complex than it looks
502.hook: kamma is not one-to-one; don't generalize from a single case
502.howItsDone: MN 135 and MN 136 sit side by side in the collection and are studied as a pair; another discourse (AN 4.77) lists the results of kamma among the things not to be speculated about.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kammadayada, Subha's seven pairs, and beings as heirs of their deeds. Your line: heirs of our deeds.

Somebody's uncle smoked two packs a day and lived to ninety-five. So, he says at every family dinner, smoking can't be that bad. One case, one big conclusion. The hundred and thirty-sixth discourse is about exactly this mistake, made by serious spiritual seekers. It opens with a misunderstanding: a wanderer named Potaliputta tells the monk Samiddhi a claim about what the Buddha teaches, Samiddhi answers too simply, and Ananda brings it all to the Buddha. So the Buddha lays out the whole thing carefully.
screen: `TWO PACKS A DAY. LIVED TO NINETY-FIVE.` → `ONE CASE, ONE BIG CONCLUSION.` → `THE BUDDHA LAYS IT OUT.`

segments.voice: Four people, the Buddha says. The first harms living beings, steals, lies, and after death is reborn in a bad state. The second does the same and is reborn in a good state. The third lives well and is reborn in a good state. The fourth lives well and is reborn in a bad state. Now imagine a meditator with a special power of vision who sees just one of these cases. Seeing the second, they conclude: there are no bad deeds; nothing comes of them. Seeing the fourth: good living is pointless. Seeing the first: everyone who harms goes to a bad state, always, and anyone who says otherwise is wrong. The Buddha agrees with what they saw. He disagrees with what they concluded. They saw a real case and turned it into a universal law. The person who harmed and still went to a good state, he says, may have done good deeds earlier, or later, or held a clear and right view at the time of death. The harmful deeds will still ripen, sometime. The same in reverse for the good person in a bad state. Deeds ripen on their own timing, mixed with everything else a person has done. So yesterday's teaching isn't a vending machine: put in a deed, get a matching result today. It's more like weather, built from many currents at once. The Buddha didn't deny the pattern. He denied the shortcut: one case, one law, and a quick verdict on a stranger.

503.title: Two joys
503.hook: joy and grief rooted in home life, and in letting go
503.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often speak of the joy of renunciation, and lay Buddhists practice small renunciations such as keeping eight precepts on observance days, giving things away, or spending days on retreat.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kamma, four people and four outcomes, and deeds that ripen on their own time. Your line: one case, not one law.

There's the joy of unboxing something new: the smell, the plastic film, the first time it turns on. And there's a different joy, harder to name: the afternoon you finally clear out a closet, and the room feels bigger, and so do you. Both are real happiness. They don't feel the same. The hundred and thirty-seventh discourse maps the mind's moods with unusual care, and in the middle of the map it does something surprising. It doesn't divide joy from sorrow. It divides joy from joy.
screen: `THE JOY OF UNBOXING.` → `THE JOY OF A CLEARED CLOSET.` → `JOY DIVIDED FROM JOY.`

segments.voice: The discourse calls the first kind joy based on the household life, in Pali gehasita somanassa. It comes from getting a pleasing sight, sound, smell, taste, touch or idea, or remembering one you had before. Nobody calls it wicked. It's just tied to having. The second kind is joy based on renunciation, nekkhamma. It comes, the text says, from seeing that sights and sounds and all the rest are impermanent, changing, passing, and seeing it with real understanding. Letting go, it turns out, has its own happiness. Grief gets the same treatment. There's grief based on household life: not getting what you want, or remembering what you lost. And grief based on renunciation: a longing for freedom, the ache of wanting to be further along the path. Then equanimity, two kinds again. That's thirty-six positions of the mind, all mapped. The instruction is gentle and step by step. Rely on the joy of letting go to set aside the joy of having. Rely on the grief of longing for freedom to set aside the grief of loss. Then rely on the equanimity of letting go, and eventually set aside even the joy. It doesn't say: stop feeling joy. It says: use a quieter, deeper joy to loosen your grip on a louder one. You don't climb out of happiness. You climb through it, into kinds that don't depend on what's in the box.
screen: `JOY FROM HAVING` · `JOY FROM LETTING GO` · `TWO GRIEFS, TWO EQUANIMITIES` · `USE THE QUIETER JOY` · then, large: `TWO JOYS.`

segments.voice: Look for a joy that doesn't come from getting anything: the ease of a long out-breath, the relief of a phone face down, the calm of not needing this moment to be anything else. It may be faint, and that's fine. Let it be noticed, and let it be enough for now.
Two joys. Joy based on home life, from having, and joy based on renunciation, from seeing clearly and letting go. Today's word.
Your line: climb through it. There's joy in having, and a quieter joy in letting go. See you tomorrow.

504.title: Not scattered, not stuck
504.hook: attention not scattered outward, not stuck inward
504.carry: neither flies off nor holds on
504.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist schools warn both against distraction and against becoming attached to pleasant meditative states, and students are taught to notice each without forcing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two joys, one from having and a quieter one from letting go. Your line: climb through it.

There are two ways to lose an afternoon. One: forty tabs open, three conversations, half-watching a video, attention flying outward in every direction. Two: stuck in your own head, replaying a comment from last week, or so absorbed in a pleasant daydream you forget to eat. One scatters, one sticks. The hundred and thirty-eighth discourse names both. The Buddha gives a short instruction and goes into his dwelling. The monks, just as with the bhaddekaratta verse, go looking for Mahakaccana.
screen: `FORTY TABS OPEN.` → `STUCK IN YOUR OWN HEAD.` → `THE MONKS GO TO MAHAKACCANA.`

segments.voice: Here's the Buddha's instruction, in paraphrase. A monk should examine things so that his consciousness isn't scattered and spread out externally, isn't stuck internally, and, not clinging, isn't agitated. Then there's no more birth, aging and death. That's all. He goes in. Mahakaccana unpacks it. Scattered outward is when the eye sees a form and consciousness follows its attractive look, tied to its pleasure, chained to it. Same for sounds, smells, tastes, touches and ideas. That's the forty tabs. Stuck inward is subtler. Someone reaches a calm, joyful meditative state and then gets attached to the joy of it, bound by its pleasure. Even good stillness can become a place to hide. And agitation from clinging? That's taking the body, feelings, perceptions, formations or consciousness as myself, and then being shaken when they change. Mahakaccana puts the middle in an unusual place. Not halfway between busy and calm, but beyond both habits: attention that can go out to the world without being dragged away, and come home without being glued there. The Buddha, hearing it, approves. Look back at the week: five messengers at Yama's court, one fine night, the verse explained, heirs of our deeds, more complex than it looks, two joys. And now a mind that neither flies off nor holds on.
screen: `A BRIEF SAYING, THEN SILENCE` · `SCATTERED: CHASING WHAT'S SEEN` · `STUCK: CLINGING TO CALM` · `AGITATED: TAKING IT AS ME` · then, large: `NOT SCATTERED, NOT STUCK.`

segments.voice: Settle on the breath, and when attention flies out to a sound, a plan, a screen, notice: scattered, and gently come back. When you find yourself sinking into a pleasant fog or circling one thought, notice: stuck, and gently open up again to the whole body, the room. Home isn't a cell; it's a doorway you can stand in.
Not scattered. Attention that isn't dragged outward by what it sees, and isn't stuck inward in its own calm. Today's word.
Your line: neither flies off nor holds on. A week of discourses ends with a mind at ease in the doorway. That's day five hundred four.
